method: All printed pages read from the supplied PDFs at 2x-3x zoom, with explicit local traversals recorded per page. Ordered source blocks include every instructional bullet, table row/cell, flowchart step, diagram label, arrow annotation, legend entry, caption, image and note. Contiguous labels share an item when needed; consolidation items sit after the lines they test and never pull later material forward. Headers, timestamps, footers and blank Active space excluded.
caveats: Ch60 p1001-1004: source checklist from existing 86 questions, each mapped to its printed line in book order. Visual scan was read at 2x-3x zoom; any printed unit errors or ambiguous glyphs are taught as printed and flagged in explanations where known. Format defects (missing blanks/malformed matches) were repaired by converting to recall format without changing the underlying fact or citation.

elements.source: ‘Portal hypertension occurs only in the presence of cirrhosis.’ [Opening line of the chapter: portal hypertension can manifest with or without cirrhosis. (Book p1001)]

Match the p1001 outcome chains — 1) Portal hypertension  2) Ascites  3) Jaundice + liver failure  4) Raised splenic pressure … A) Average survival without transplant printed as ‘a years’  B) Leads to hepatorenal syndrome  C) Hepatic encephalopathy and variceal bleeding  D) Splenomegaly and thrombocytopenia [Portal hypertension leads to hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites; ascites (1st sign of decompensation) leads to hepatorenal syndrome]
The 1st sign of decompensation in portal hypertension is: [Under the bullet ‘ascites’ the page states ‘1st sign of decompensation’. (Book p1001)]
Portal hypertension is defined by a portal venous pressure of: [Pathogenesis line: portal venous pressure ≥ 12 mm Hg. (Book p1001)]
Sinusoidal pressure is defined as ≥ 6 mm Hg; it becomes clinically significant at: [‘Sinusoidal pressure ≥ 6 mm Hg (clinically significant if ≥ 10 mm Hg)’. (Book p1001)]

A 48-year-old with biopsy-proven cirrhosis has a spleen 4 cm below the costal margin and a platelet count of 90,000/µL. Which pair gives the earliest clinical and earliest biochemical manifestations of portal hypertension? [Raised splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). (Book p1001)]
The mean survival without decompensation or transplant in portal hypertension is: [‘Mean survival without decompensation / transplant : 12 years’. (Book p1001)]

After decompensation (jaundice + liver failure), average survival without transplant is about: [The page prints ‘Decompensation : Average survival a years without transplant’ — the ‘a’ is a typographical slip for 1, i.e. about 1 year, in contrast]

All but one of the following are listed under ‘Portal hypertension leads to’. The odd one out is: [The three listed consequences are hepatic encephalopathy, variceal bleeding and ascites; hepatomegaly is not listed. (Book p1001)]

‘Thrombocytopenia is the earliest clinical manifestation of portal hypertension.’ [Raised splenic pressure → splenomegaly (earliest clinical) and thrombocytopenia (earliest biochemical). (Book p1001)]

Match the cirrhotic-sinusoid diagram events of p1001 to the structures — 1) Deposition of collagen  2) Activation  3) Constriction  4) Defenestration … A) Sinusoids  B) Hepatic stellate cells  C) Space of Disse  D) Sinusoidal lumen/fenestrae [Diagram labels: deposition of collagen in space of Disse; activation of hepatic stellate cells; constriction of sinusoids; defenestration of sinusoids]
In cirrhosis, collagen deposition in the hepatic sinusoid occurs in the: [The diagram labels ‘Deposition of collagen in space of Disse’. (Book p1001)]
Which cell is labelled as activated in the cirrhotic sinusoid of p1001? [‘Activation of hepatic stellate cells’ is labelled in the cirrhotic panel. (Book p1001)]

‘Fenestrae of the sinusoidal endothelium are preserved in cirrhosis.’ [The cirrhotic panel labels ‘Defenestration of sinusoids’ and the summary line reads ‘Disappearance of fenestration in cirrhosis’. (Book p1001)]

In a cirrhotic liver, the direct mechanical mechanism by which regenerating nodules raise portal pressure, as drawn on p1001, is: [‘Nodule and fibrous septation compress sinusoids → leads to ↑ portal pressure → ↑ splenic vein pressure’. (Book p1001)]

The portal vein is formed behind the neck of the pancreas by the junction of the splenic vein and the: [Formation: splenic vein and superior mesenteric veins join behind the neck of pancreas. (Book p1001)]
The portal vein develops from the: [Development: ‘Inferior segment of left and right vitelline veins joins to form portal vein’. (Book p1001)]
The length of the portal vein given on p1001 is: [Under formation: ‘7.5 cm long’. (Book p1001)]
The haemodynamic character of the portal vein stated on p1001 is: [‘Portal vein has high compliance low resistance’. (Book p1001)]

Match the portal-branching diagram labels of p1001 — 1) Umbilical vein  2) Cystic vein  3) 1st order portal vein  4) 3rd order portal vein (Bifurcation) … A) Bifurcates in the lobe  B) Main trunk  C) Drains into the right portal vein  D) Drains into the left portal vein [‘Umbilical vein drains into left portal vein’, ‘Cystic vein drains into right portal vein’, 1st order portal vein is the main trunk, and the 3rd order]

Hepatic ischaemia remains rare in portal hypertension because of the hepatic buffer response — its basis on p1001 is: [Note: hepatic buffer response — hepatic ischaemia is rare d/t dual blood supply, portal vein / hepatic artery. (Book p1001)]

At the hilum, the portal vein lies with respect to the hepatic artery and bile duct — the relation stated on p1001 is: [Under formation: ‘Hilum posterior to hepatic and bile duct’ — the portal vein lies posterior to the hepatic artery and bile duct. (Book p1001)]

elements.source: In the equation P = F × R used on p1002 for portal HTN, a rise in sinusoidal resistance leads to: [Resistance due to: (P = F × R; R↑ = P↑). (Book p1002)]

Match the HVPG (hepatic venous pressure gradient) ladder of p1002 — 1) 1–5 mm Hg  2) ≥ 10 mm Hg  3) ≥ 12 mm Hg  4) ≥ 20 mm Hg … A) Threshold pressure for variceal rupture  B) Normal value  C) ↑ Risk of death  D) Clinically significant portal hypertension [HVPG table: 1–5 mm Hg = normal value; ≥ 10 mm Hg = clinically significant portal hypertension; ≥ 12 mm Hg = threshold pressure for variceal rupture; ≥]
The HVPG that marks the threshold pressure for variceal rupture is: [≥ 12 mm Hg is labelled the threshold pressure for variceal rupture. (Book p1002)]

A cirrhotic patient's HVPG is measured at 11 mm Hg. According to the p1002 ladder, the best interpretation is: [≥ 10 mm Hg = clinically significant portal hypertension; ≥ 12 mm Hg = threshold for variceal rupture; so 11 sits between the two printed marks. (Book ]
The functional (non-mechanical) cause of sinusoidal vasoconstriction in portal HTN is a fall in: [Functional cause: ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration. (Book p1002)]
‘In sinusoidal vasoconstriction, the NO pathway causes the sinusoid to relax.’ [Functional cause: ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration. (Book p1002)]
The mechanical cause of sinusoidal resistance in portal HTN, as drawn on p1002, is: [Mechanical cause: nodule compressing sinusoid (functional arm is the ↓ NO pathway). (Book p1002)]

All but one of the following appear in the p1002 functional-cause chain (↓ intrasinusoidal NO → …). The odd one out is: [The chain is ↓ intrasinusoidal NO → contraction of sinusoid → defenestration; portal vein thrombosis is not part of it. (Book p1002)]
Pre-hepatic portal hypertension corresponds to occlusion of the: [Pre-hepatic: first order portal vein occlusion AKA extrahepaticportal venous obstruction (EHPVO). (Book p1002)]
EHPVO is characteristically seen in: [Pre-hepatic (EHPVO) — ‘seen in 3-8 yr olds’. (Book p1002)]

Match the printed features of EHPVO — 1) Bleed  2) Spleen  3) Liver  4) Prognosis … A) No cirrhosis  B) Massive splenomegaly  C) Severe upper gastrointestinal  D) Good [Characteristic features: severe upper gastrointestinal bleed, massive splenomegaly; no cirrhosis (good prognosis). (Book p1002)]
Post-hepatic portal hypertension, cause ‘a’, is hepatic vein obstruction, also known as: [Post-hepatic a. cause: hepatic vein obstruction AKA Budd Chiari syndrome. (Book p1002)]
The classical findings of Budd–Chiari syndrome printed on p1002 are ascites and: [Classical findings: ascites, hepatomegaly (note: hepatomegaly, not splenomegaly). (Book p1002)]

Match the post-hepatic ‘other causes’ (right heart failure) of p1002 — 1) Valvular  2) Myocardial  3) Pericardial … A) Constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP)  B) Restrictive cardiomyopathy  C) Tricuspid regurgitation [Right heart failure: tricuspid regurgitation, restrictive cardiomyopathy, constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP). (Book p1002)]

A patient with constrictive pericarditis and a raised JVP develops ascites and portal pressure elevation. In the p1002 classification this falls under: [Constrictive pericarditis (↑ JVP) is listed under post-hepatic → b. other causes → right heart failure. (Book p1002)]
Which of the following is the RARE cause of EHPVO listed on p1002? [Causes: umbilical sepsis (listed without qualifier) and splenic vein thrombosis (rare). (Book p1002)]

In the p1002 diagram, the intrahepatic branch of portal HTN is drawn at the level of the: [The arrow from ‘Intrahepatic’ is labelled (3rd order portal vein) and then splits into pre-sinusoidal, post-sinusoidal and sinusoidal. (Book p1002)]
Intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal cause ‘a’ is NCPF, which stands for: [Pre-sinusoidal a. NCPF (Non cirrhotic portal fibrosis) / Idiopathic portal hypertension. (Book p1002)]

NCPF / idiopathic portal hypertension typically presents as a young adult with upper GI bleed and splenomegaly, and cirrhosis is: [Presentation: young adult with upper GI bleed, splenomegaly, cirrhosis (rare). (Book p1002)]

A day 20 post-allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant patient on a myeloablative alkylator-based regimen develops tender hepatomegaly and weight gain. The p1002 entity to suspect is: [Post-sinusoidal cause: sinusoidal obstruction syndrome / veno-occlusive disease a/w post hematopoietic stem cell transplant following myeloablative th]
After myeloablative therapy with alkylating agents, symptoms of veno-occlusive disease appear: [The diagram shows the arrow labelled (10 – 30 days after) leading to symptoms. (Book p1002)]

All but one of the following are listed as intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal causes on p1002. The odd one out is: [Pre-sinusoidal: NCPF/idiopathic portal hypertension, schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis. Budd–Chiari is post-hepatic, not intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal. (Book]
The intrahepatic sinusoidal cause of portal hypertension on p1002 is: [Sinusoidal: cause — cirrhosis (post-sinusoidal is SOS/VOD; pre-sinusoidal is NCPF etc.). (Book p1002)]
The granulomatous ‘other cause’ of intrahepatic pre-sinusoidal portal HTN on p1002 is: [b. Other causes: schistosomiasis (parasitic) and sarcoidosis (granulomatous). (Book p1002)]

elements.source: In the p1003 work-up flow, the step ‘Deranged LFT + USG : fatty liver + negative serology’ is qualified by: [Flow: deranged LFT + USG : fatty liver + negative serology (AST / ALT < 150) → confirms chronic hepatitis (NASH). (Book p1003)]
The Fibroscan value in the p1003 flow that leads to the diagnosis of cirrhosis is: [Flow: confirms chronic hepatitis (NASH) → Fibroscan : 13.5 kPa → cirrhosis. (Book p1003)]
After cirrhosis is established in the flow, the pair of findings that establishes portal hypertension (+) is: [Flow: cirrhosis → splenomegaly (+), ↓ platelet → portal hypertension (+). (Book p1003)]
Portal HTN is quantified with HVPG, where: [Quantity with HVPG: HVPG = WHVP − FHVP. (Book p1003)]

Match the p1003 abbreviations — 1) HVPG  2) WHVP  3) FHVP … A) Wedged hepatic venous pressure  B) Free hepatic venous pressure  C) Hepatic venous pressure gradient [HVPG : hepatic venous pressure gradient; WHVP : wedged hepatic venous pressure; FHVP : free hepatic venous pressure. (Book p1003)]

‘On p1003 the expansion line prints the free pressure as “FWVP : Free hepatic venous pressure”, while the formula line prints HVPG = WHVP − FHVP.’ [The expansion line is printed ‘FWVP : Free hepatic venous pressure’ whereas the formula is ‘HVPG = WHVP − FHVP’; both denote the free hepatic venous p]

A child with EHPVO has large oesophageal varices but a normal HVPG. Which row of the p1003 table explains why HVPG fails here? [Prehepatic: normal / normal / normal — the gradient across the liver is normal because the obstruction is before the liver. (Book p1003)]

‘In the p1003 flow, portal hypertension (+) is established only by endoscopy.’ [Flow: cirrhosis → splenomegaly (+), ↓ platelet → portal hypertension (+), which then branches to quantity with HVPG and endoscopy. (Book p1003)]

Match the p1003 table locations with their pressure patterns — 1) Presinusoidal  2) Sinusoidal  3) The row where the hepatic vein cannot be cannulated … A) WHVP increased, FHVP increased, HVPG normal  B) WHVP, FHVP and HVPG all normal  C) WHVP increased, FHVP normal, HVPG increased [Presinusoidal: normal/normal/normal; sinusoidal: increased/normal/increased; the unlabeled row: increased / increased (hepatic vein cannot be cannulat]
The prehepatic and presinusoidal rows of the p1003 table are identical: WHVP, FHVP and HVPG are all: [Both the prehepatic and presinusoidal rows print Normal in all three columns. (Book p1003)]
In the sinusoidal (cirrhotic) row of the table, WHVP is increased while FHVP remains: [Sinusoidal: WHVP increased, FHVP normal, HVPG increased. (Book p1003)]

In a patient with Budd–Chiari syndrome the hepatic vein cannot be cannulated. Which p1003 table row fits this situation, and what does it predict for HVPG? [The unlabeled row: WHVP increased, FHVP increased (hepatic vein cannot be cannulated), HVPG normal — the pattern of post-hepatic obstruction. (Book p1]
‘In presinusoidal portal hypertension the HVPG is increased according to the p1003 table.’ [Presinusoidal row: normal / normal / normal. (Book p1003)]
In the p1003 flow, an HVPG > 10 mm Hg prompts Rx with the non-selective β-blocker labelled (best): [Bracket on the table: > 10 mm Hg → Rx non-selective β-blocker : carvedilol (best). (Book p1003)]
Endoscopy showing large varices → p1003 Rx of choice is the non-selective β-blocker: [Large varices → Rx non-selective β-blocker : carvedilol (best). (Book p1003)]
Endoscopy showing mild/moderate varices is handled by: [Endoscopy arms: large varices → non-selective β-blocker; mild/moderate varices → conservative management. (Book p1003)]

Match the p1003 indications for endoscopic variceal ligation — 1) Intolerant to β-blocker therapy  2) β-blockers contraindicated  3) Target HVPG not achieved … A) With β-blocker  B) Severe bradycardia  C) Asthma, COPD [Intolerant to β-blocker therapy: asthma, COPD; β-blockers contraindicated: severe bradycardia; target HVPG not achieved with β-blocker. (Book p1003)]

A cirrhotic with large varices develops a resting heart rate of 42 bpm after starting a β-blocker. According to p1003, endoscopic variceal ligation is indicated here under which heading? [Severe bradycardia is the printed example under ‘β-blockers contraindicated’; intolerance refers to asthma/COPD. (Book p1003)]

Match the modified Child–Pugh parameters of p1003 — 1) Ascites  2) Encephalopathy  3) Albumin  4) Prothrombin time … A) Seconds increased  B) Hepatic synthetic protein  C) Fluid in the peritoneal cavity  D) Altered sensorium [Parameters assessed: ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (seconds increased). (Book p1003)]
In the modified Child–Pugh classes A, B, C of p1003, the bracketed classes that require transplant are: [Classes: A, B, C — the bracket over B and C is annotated ‘Requires transplant’. (Book p1003)]

All but one of the following are parameters of the modified Child–Pugh system on p1003. The odd one out is: [Parameters: ascites, encephalopathy, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time (seconds increased) — creatinine is not listed. (Book p1003)]

elements.source: The main factor in variceal bleeds, as stated on p1004, is: [Determinants: main factor — variceal wall tension. (Book p1004)]

Match the p1004 determinants of variceal bleeding — 1) Main factor  2) Vessel component  3) Pressure component  4) The bracketed note on diameter + pressure … A) Pressure  B) Variceal wall tension  C) Vessel diameter  D) Directly related to HVPG [Main factor: variceal wall tension; determined by vessel diameter + pressure; bracket: directly related to HVPG. (Book p1004)]

The p1004 line ‘Gastric esophageal varices : 50% cause cirrhosis’ attributes varices to cirrhosis in what proportion (as printed)? [Causes: gastric esophageal varices : 50% cause cirrhosis (as printed). (Book p1004)]
The development rate of varices in patients without varices, per p1004, is: [Causes: without varices development rate : 8% per year. (Book p1004)]
The variceal hemorrhage occurrence rate given on p1004 is: [Causes: variceal hemorrhage occurrence rate : 5–15% per year. (Book p1004)]

Match the p1004 risk-of-bleeding figures with the varix size — 1) Small varices (≤ 5 mm)  2) Large varices … A) 30%/year  B) < 10%/year [Risk of bleeding: small varices (≤ 5 mm) : < 10%/year; large varices : 30%/year. (Book p1004)]
Mortality from variceal bleeding, as printed on p1004, is: [Causes: mortality from variceal bleeding : 15–30%. (Book p1004)]

A cirrhotic is found to have large oesophageal varices on screening. Using only the p1004 figures, the pair that describes his annual bleed risk and the case-fatality if a bleed occurs is: [Large varices : 30%/year risk; mortality from variceal bleeding : 15–30%. (Book p1004)]

A patient presents with acute variceal bleeding. The immediate access step in the p1004 flow is: [Acute variceal bleeding flow starts with a large bore IV cannulas alongside the drug arms. (Book p1004)]
The 1st-line vasoactive drug labelled (1st) in the p1004 flow is: [Terlipressin (1st) is the printed first-line arm; octreotide follows after the ‘>’ as the alternative. (Book p1004)]
The terlipressin regimen in the p1004 flow is: [Printed as ‘a mg stat dose → a mg Q6h × 48 hours’ — the dose figure is degraded in the print; the intended regimen is the 2 mg stat → 2 mg Q6h × 48 ho]
The octreotide alternative in the p1004 flow is: [> IV Octreotide 50 µg stat → 50 µg/hour. (Book p1004)]

‘In the p1004 flow, IV octreotide is the labelled first-line drug and terlipressin is the alternative.’ [Terlipressin (1st) is the first arm; the ‘>’ leads to the IV octreotide 50 µg stat → 50 µg/hour alternative. (Book p1004)]

Match the three bullets in the p1004 resuscitation box — 1) Infection prophylaxis  2) Volume  3) Airway … A) Intubation to be considered  B) Replace blood volume  C) Start antibiotics [Box: start antibiotics; replace blood volume; intubation to be considered. (Book p1004)]

A variceal-bleed patient is obtunded and gagless on arrival. Which bullet of the p1004 box is activated by this finding? [Airway protection: intubation to be considered is the third bullet of the box. (Book p1004)]
Upon failure of drug therapy and resuscitation, the p1004 flow proceeds to endoscopy for: [Upon failure → endoscopy : variceal ligation or sclerotherapy. (Book p1004)]
Upon failure of endoscopy, the final step of the p1004 ladder is: [Upon failure → TIPSS (Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt). (Book p1004)]

All but one of the following are bullets in the p1004 resuscitation box. The odd one out is: [The box holds: start antibiotics, replace blood volume, intubation to be considered — the octreotide infusion belongs to the drug arm, not the box. (B]

A cirrhotic bleeds from varices; terlipressin + resuscitation fail, and endoscopic ligation fails. The next rung of the p1004 ladder is: [Ladder: drugs → (upon failure) endoscopy : ligation or sclerotherapy → (upon failure) TIPSS. (Book p1004)]
